part_title: CodeArtifact Security and Event-Driven Package Validation

scenes.title: CodeArtifact Cross-Account Authorization
scenes.narration: This architecture has a producer account that owns a CodeArtifact domain and repository, and a consumer account whose build role needs to download a package. Follow the three stages. First, the consumer role requests a CodeArtifact authorisation token. The domain owner's resource policy and the caller's identity permissions must allow the supported GetAuthorizationToken operation. The caller also needs permission for the relevant STS service bearer token operation. Next the temporary token is returned. The build tool then uses it to authenticate package download requests, which are separately authorised for repository read access. The slide highlights distinct domain and repository resource policies because a token alone is not permission to every repository. Scope the trusted principal to the intended build role and restrict readable repositories. An explicit Deny overrides other allows. This is a useful pattern for central dependency management across AWS accounts: developers and CI builds consume approved package versions without embedding permanent registry passwords or making the repository public.

scenes.title: CodeArtifact Package Events and Safe Automation
scenes.narration: This final workflow starts when CodeArtifact records a package-version state change and EventBridge matches that event. The event initiates a validation pipeline, not an unconditional approval to deploy. A build job retrieves the new version, runs dependency scanning, security and policy checks, and executes unit or integration tests. If any validation fails, the automation stops and does not publish a release. If the checks pass, it proposes an updated pinned dependency version for review, and only the approved change is merged and released. The right side stresses duplicate-event handling: event deliveries can be repeated, so use an idempotency key such as package name, version and revision to avoid triggering duplicate builds or approvals. Do not trust an upstream package solely because it exists in a private repository. Keep integrity checks, dependency provenance, allowed upstreams and review controls in the supply chain. This makes CodeArtifact part of a secure CI/CD workflow rather than merely an alternate package download URL.
